subject: maths
title: Histograms and stem-and-leaf plots
summary: Group numerical data into class intervals, then draw and read histograms and ordered stem-and-leaf plots, including split stems.
body:
How long does it take students to get to school? How tall are the players in a basketball league? When you have lots of numbers, a list is hard to read. **Histograms** and **stem-and-leaf plots** organise numerical data so you can see at a glance where most values sit — they're used in sport, health reports, weather records and the news.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can group numerical data into class intervals, draw and read a histogram, and draw and read an ordered stem-and-leaf plot (including split stems).

## Before you start

You need dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots from *Comparing data sets (Year 8)* and percentages from *Percentage of a quantity (Year 7)*.

**Warm-up**

1. In a stem-and-leaf plot with key 3 | 4 means 34, what number is stem 5, leaf 0? *(Answer: 50)*
2. What is 12 out of 40 as a percentage? *(Answer: 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%)*

## Think of it like this

### Sorting mail into pigeonholes

A school office sorts letters into pigeonholes: one hole for surnames A–E, one for F–J, and so on. Once sorted, you can see straight away which hole is the fullest. A histogram does the same with numbers: each value goes into a "hole" (a class interval), and the height of each bar shows how full that hole is.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* once a letter is in a pigeonhole you can still read its name, but once a number is in a histogram bar you can no longer see its exact value — a histogram only shows how many values are in each interval.

## Key ideas

### Grouping data into class intervals

When numerical data has many different values, we group it into **class intervals** of equal width, such as 0 to less than 10, 10 to less than 20, 20 to less than 30. The **class width** is 10. Every value must fit into exactly one class, so a value on a boundary (like 20) goes into the class that *starts* at 20. A **frequency table** lists each class and its **frequency** (how many values are in it).

### Histograms

A **histogram** is a column graph for grouped numerical data:

- The horizontal axis is a number line showing the class boundaries.
- The vertical axis shows frequency.
- The bars **touch**, because the classes join with no gaps — one class ends exactly where the next begins.
- The tallest bar shows the **modal class** (the class with the highest frequency).

![A histogram of the heights of 30 students with classes of width 5 cm from 150 to 180 cm; the frequencies are 2, 5, 9, 8, 4 and 2](/diagrams/y9/maths/histograms-and-stem-and-leaf-plots-parts.svg)

In this histogram, 9 students are 160 cm to less than 165 cm tall, so that is the modal class. Adding all the bar heights gives the total: 2 + 5 + 9 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 30 students.

### Stem-and-leaf plots

A **stem-and-leaf plot** splits each value into a **stem** (here the tens digit) and a **leaf** (the units digit). An **ordered** plot has its leaves in order from smallest to largest, and it always has a **key**, such as 3 | 5 means 35. Unlike a histogram, a stem-and-leaf plot keeps every original value.

Turn a stem-and-leaf plot on its side and the rows of leaves look like the bars of a histogram with classes of width 10 — so it shows the shape of the data too.

### Split stems

When most values have the same few stems, the plot is too squashed. A **split stem** uses each stem twice: the first row holds leaves 0–4 and the second holds leaves 5–9.

| Stem | Leaf |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2 3 |
| 4 | 6 8 9 |
| 5 | 0 1 1 4 |
| 5 | 5 7 |

Key: 4 | 2 means 42. The values are 42, 43, 46, 48, 49, 50, 51, 51, 54, 55, 57.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

The travel times (in minutes) of 24 students are:
12, 25, 8, 31, 17, 22, 45, 19, 28, 14, 36, 20, 9, 27, 33, 16, 24, 41, 18, 30, 26, 11, 38, 23.
Make a frequency table using classes of width 10, then draw a histogram.

Step 1: choose the classes — the smallest value is 8 and the largest is 45, so use 0 to less than 10 up to 40 to less than 50.
Step 2: tally each value into its class — 20 goes in "20 to less than 30" and 30 goes in "30 to less than 40", because a boundary value belongs to the class that starts with it.

| Travel time (min) | Frequency |
|---|---|
| 0 to less than 10 | 2 |
| 10 to less than 20 | 7 |
| 20 to less than 30 | 8 |
| 30 to less than 40 | 5 |
| 40 to less than 50 | 2 |

Step 3: check the total — 2 + 7 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 24 ✓, the same as the number of students.
Step 4: draw touching bars with these heights.

![A histogram of travel times of 24 students in classes of width 10 minutes from 0 to 50; the frequencies are 2, 7, 8, 5 and 2](/diagrams/y9/maths/histograms-and-stem-and-leaf-plots-ex1.svg)

### Example 2

Use the heights histogram in Key ideas. (a) How many students are 165 cm or taller? (b) What percentage is that?

Step 1: find the bars that start at 165 or more — 165 to less than 170 (8), 170 to less than 175 (4), 175 to less than 180 (2).
Step 2: add them — 8 + 4 + 2 = **14 students**.
Step 3: total students = 30, so the percentage is 14 ÷ 30 × 100 ≈ **46.7%** — to compare part with the whole.

### Example 3

Scores in a reaction game: 23, 41, 35, 18, 29, 44, 37, 31, 26, 52, 38, 33, 47, 29, 35. Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf plot, find the range, and count the scores of 40 or more.

Step 1: stems are the tens digits 1 to 5. Write each leaf next to its stem, then put each row's leaves in order.

| Stem | Leaf |
|---|---|
| 1 | 8 |
| 2 | 3 6 9 9 |
| 3 | 1 3 5 5 7 8 |
| 4 | 1 4 7 |
| 5 | 2 |

Key: 2 | 3 means 23.

Step 2: count the leaves — 1 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 15 ✓.
Step 3: range = largest − smallest = 52 − 18 = **34**.
Step 4: scores of 40 or more are in rows 4 and 5: 41, 44, 47, 52, so **4 scores**.

Turned on its side, the plot matches this histogram:

![A histogram of 15 game scores with classes of width 10 from 10 to 60; the frequencies are 1, 4, 6, 3 and 1](/diagrams/y9/maths/histograms-and-stem-and-leaf-plots-ex3.svg)

## Common mistakes

- **Putting a boundary value in the wrong class.** 30 belongs in "30 to less than 40", not "20 to less than 30". Fix: a class includes its starting value but not its end value.
- **Leaving gaps between histogram bars.** Gaps suggest separate categories. Fix: bars touch because the classes join.
- **Giving the frequency instead of the class.** The modal class is an interval such as "160 to less than 165", not the number 9.
- **Forgetting the key or not ordering the leaves.** Without a key, 3 | 5 could mean 35 or 3.5. Fix: always order the leaves and write a key.
- **Counting a repeated leaf once.** Leaves 2 2 mean the value appears twice — count both.

## Tips to remember

- **"Start in, end out"** (made-up memory trick): a class includes the number it starts at, but not the number it ends at.
- **Histogram = no gaps.** If you can see daylight between the bars, it's a column graph, not a histogram.
- **Stem-and-leaf keeps the leaves on the tree** (made-up): every original value survives; a histogram only keeps the counts.
- **Check your total:** the frequencies (or the leaves) must add up to the number of data values.

## Key terms

- **Class interval** — a group of values, such as 20 to less than 30, used to sort numerical data.
- **Class width** — the size of each class interval (for example 10).
- **Frequency** — how many data values fall in a class.
- **Frequency table** — a table listing each class and its frequency.
- **Histogram** — a graph of grouped numerical data with touching bars whose heights are frequencies.
- **Modal class** — the class interval with the highest frequency.
- **Stem-and-leaf plot** — a display that splits each value into a stem and a leaf and keeps every original value.
- **Split stem** — a stem used twice, once for leaves 0–4 and once for leaves 5–9.

## Summary

- Group numerical data into equal class intervals; a boundary value goes in the class that starts with it.
- A histogram has a number-line horizontal axis, frequency on the vertical axis and touching bars.
- The tallest bar shows the modal class; adding all bar heights gives the total.
- An ordered stem-and-leaf plot keeps every value and needs a key; split stems spread out squashed data.
- Always check that the frequencies add up to the number of values.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows how many hours 40 students slept last night. How many students slept 8 to less than 9 hours?
questions.explanation: The bar from 8 to 9 hours reaches a frequency of 11. The tempting 13 is the tallest bar, which is the class 7 to less than 8 hours.
steps: Find the bar that starts at 8 and ends at 9 on the horizontal axis.
Read its height on the frequency axis: 11 students.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 13 is the bar for 7 to less than 8 hours. Find the bar that starts at 8 and ends at 9.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 8 is the class boundary on the horizontal axis. Read the height of the bar on the vertical axis.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 19 = 11 + 6 + 2 is everyone who slept 8 hours or more. Read only the one bar from 8 to 9.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of hours of sleep for 40 students, classes of width 1 hour from 5 to 11, with frequencies 2, 6, 13, 11, 6 and 2

questions.prompt:
An ordered stem-and-leaf plot has key 3 | 2 means 32.
1 | 5 8
2 | 0 4 4 9
3 | 2 3 6 6 6
4 | 1 5 7
5 | 0
What is the largest value, and how many values are there?
questions.explanation: The bottom row, stem 5 with leaf 0, is 50, and there are 2 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 15 leaves. Counting the stems (5) instead of the leaves is the usual slip.
steps: The largest value is in the last row: stem 5, leaf 0, so 50.
Count the leaves, one per value: 2 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 15.

mistakes.A: Step 1: a stem and a leaf together make one value. Stem 5 with leaf 0 is 50, not 5.
mistakes.C: Step 2: there are 5 stems, but each leaf is one value. Count the leaves.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the last row (stem 5, leaf 0) is also a value. Read the bottom row.

questions.prompt: Why do the bars of a histogram touch each other?

options.A: To fit more bars across the page
options.B: Because every class has the same frequency
options.C: The classes join with no gaps — each class ends exactly where the next one begins
options.D: Because the data are categories, like favourite colours

questions.explanation: A histogram shows numerical data on a number line split into classes that join, so the bars touch. Category data (like colours) uses a column graph with gaps.
steps: A histogram is for numerical data grouped into class intervals.
The intervals join with no gaps (for example 10 to less than 20, then 20 to less than 30), so the bars touch.

mistakes.A: Step 1: it is not about saving space. Think about what the horizontal axis shows: a continuous number line.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the bars can have different heights. Touching is about the classes on the horizontal axis.
mistakes.D: Step 1: categories are drawn as a column graph WITH gaps. Histograms are for grouped numerical data.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the ages of 40 people at a movie session. How many people were aged 30 or older?
questions.explanation: The bars from 30 upwards have heights 7, 3 and 2, so 12 people. Using only the 30–40 bar (7) misses the older people.
steps: "30 or older" means every bar that starts at 30 or more: 30–40, 40–50 and 50–60.
Add their heights: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 7 is only the 30 to less than 40 bar. People aged 40 and over are also "30 or older".
mistakes.B: Step 1: you included the 20 to less than 30 bar. Start at the bar that begins at 30.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 28 is the number YOUNGER than 30. Add the bars from 30 upwards.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of ages of 40 people, classes of width 10 years from 0 to 60, with frequencies 4, 9, 15, 7, 3 and 2

questions.prompt: Data: 14, 22, 30, 27, 19, 35, 20, 29, 41, 30, 25, 18. How many values belong in the class "20 to less than 30"?
questions.explanation: The values 22, 27, 20, 29 and 25 are at least 20 and less than 30, so 5. Including the two 30s gives 7, but 30 starts the next class.
steps: The class holds values from 20 up to, but not including, 30.
Pick them out: 22, 27, 20, 29, 25 (not 30 or 30).
Count: 5 values.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 30 is not "less than 30", so both 30s belong in the next class. Leave them out.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 20 does belong here — a class includes the value it starts at. Count the 20.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you counted the class 30 to less than 40 (30, 35, 30). Count values from 20 up to, but not including, 30.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the times (in seconds) 40 students took to run 100 m. What is the modal class?
questions.explanation: The tallest bar (frequency 12) sits over 15 to less than 16 seconds. The 14–15 bar is close (11) but shorter.
steps: Find the tallest bar: it reaches 12.
Read the interval under it: 15 to less than 16 seconds.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 12 is the frequency of the tallest bar. The modal class is the interval under that bar.
mistakes.B: Step 1: this bar (11) is slightly shorter. Compare the heights carefully — the tallest reaches 12.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the modal class is the one with the TALLEST bar, not the largest times.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of 100 m times for 40 students, classes of width 1 second from 12 to 18, with frequencies 3, 8, 11, 12, 5 and 1

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the daily screen time of 50 students. What percentage of the students had at least 4 hours of screen time?
questions.explanation: 9 + 5 = 14 students had at least 4 hours, and 14 ÷ 50 × 100 = 28%. Giving 14% forgets to divide by the total.
steps: "At least 4 hours" = the bars from 4 to 5 and 5 to 6: 9 + 5 = 14 students.
Total students = 3 + 7 + 14 + 12 + 9 + 5 = 50.
Percentage = 14 ÷ 50 × 100 = 28%.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you used only the 4 to less than 5 bar. "At least 4" also includes the 5 to less than 6 bar.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 14 is the number of students. Divide by the total of 50 and multiply by 100.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you started at 3 hours. "At least 4 hours" starts at the bar beginning at 4.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of daily screen time for 50 students, classes of width 1 hour from 0 to 6, with frequencies 3, 7, 14, 12, 9 and 5

questions.prompt:
This stem-and-leaf plot uses split stems (key 6 | 1 means 61). The first row for each stem holds leaves 0–4 and the second holds leaves 5–9.
6 | 1 3 4
6 | 5 5 8 9
7 | 0 2 2 3
7 | 6 7 9
8 | 0 4
How many values are at least 70 but less than 75?
questions.explanation: The first stem-7 row (leaves 0–4) holds 70, 72, 72 and 73: 4 values. Counting both 7 rows (7) includes 76, 77 and 79.
steps: Values from 70 to 74 are in the FIRST row with stem 7: leaves 0 2 2 3.
Count every leaf, including the repeated 2: 70, 72, 72, 73 — 4 values.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the second 7 row holds 76, 77 and 79, which are not less than 75. Use only the first 7 row.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the leaf 2 appears twice, so 72 is two values. Count every leaf.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 11 is every value less than 75. Start at 70.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the number of minutes 45 people waited for a bus, but the bar for 20 to less than 30 minutes is missing. What is its height?
questions.explanation: The visible bars add to 6 + 11 + 9 + 4 = 30, so the missing bar is 45 − 30 = 15. Answering 30 stops before subtracting.
steps: Add the bars you can see: 6 + 11 + 9 + 4 = 30.
All the bars must add to 45 people.
Missing bar = 45 − 30 = 15.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 30 is the total of the bars you CAN see. Subtract it from 45.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added 45 and 30. The missing bar is the total minus the bars you can see.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the missing bar does not have to match its neighbour. Use the total of 45.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of waiting times for 45 people, classes of width 10 minutes from 0 to 50; the bars are labelled 6, 11, a missing bar marked with a question mark for 20 to less than 30, then 9 and 4

questions.prompt: A histogram shows the whole-number ages of 20 people in groups 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39 and 40–44. Every group has at least one person. What is the GREATEST possible range of the ages?
questions.explanation: The youngest could be 20 and the oldest could be 44, so the greatest possible range is 44 − 20 = 24. Using 45 − 20 = 25 forgets that 44 is the top of the last group.
steps: A histogram hides the exact ages, so think about the most extreme possibilities.
Youngest possible age: 20 (bottom of 20–24). Oldest possible age: 44 (top of 40–44).
Greatest possible range = 44 − 20 = 24.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the oldest group is 40–44, so the largest possible age is 44, not 45.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you used the starts of the first and last groups. The oldest person could be 44.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 40 − 24 = 16 is the SMALLEST possible range. For the greatest, use the youngest possible and oldest possible ages.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of ages of 20 people in groups 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39 and 40–44 with frequencies 2, 5, 7, 4 and 2

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the whole-number test marks of 25 students. From the histogram alone, how many students scored MORE than 75?
questions.explanation: All 3 students in 80–89 scored above 75; any number from 0 to 5 of the 70–79 group could have too, so between 3 and 8. "Exactly 8" assumes all of the 70–79 group scored above 75.
steps: The 80–89 bar (3 students) is definitely above 75.
The 70–79 bar (5 students) could hold anywhere from 0 to 5 students above 75 — the histogram hides exact marks.
So the number is at least 3 and at most 3 + 5 = 8.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the 70–79 bar includes marks like 70 to 75, which are not more than 75. You cannot be sure all 5 are above 75.
mistakes.B: Step 2: some of the 70–79 students could have scored 76 to 79. You cannot be sure none did.
mistakes.D: Step 2: assuming half of the 70–79 group gives 2.5 students — you cannot have half a student, and the histogram does not say how they are spread.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of test marks of 25 students in groups 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79 and 80–89 with frequencies 3, 6, 8, 5 and 3

questions.prompt: A data set of 38 whole numbers has smallest value 12 and largest value 87. You group it into classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 and so on, just far enough to include every value. How many classes do you need?
questions.explanation: 12 is in 10–19 and 87 is in 80–89, so the classes are 10–19, 20–29, …, 80–89: 8 classes. Dividing the range by 10 (7.5) does not count them.
steps: 12 belongs in 10–19 and 87 belongs in 80–89.
That is 8 classes.

mistakes.A: Step 1: (87 − 12) ÷ 10 = 7.5 does not count classes. List them from 10–19 to the one that holds 87.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you counted the class boundaries 10, 20, …, 90 (9 numbers). Count the classes between them.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the number of values (38) does not decide the classes. Start at the class holding 12 and end at the class holding 87.
